---
title: "Dams mark drought vulnerability rather than buffer it, and storage cannot offset a falling water supply in Chile"
author:
  - name: Francisco Zambrano Bigiarini
    affiliations:
      - name: Universidad de Las Américas
        id: 1

abstract: |
  Expanding reservoir storage is the reflexive policy response to intensifying drought, yet
  whether dams build resilience or merely mark where vulnerability already concentrates
  remains untested under sustained drying. We treat reservoir presence as a basin-level
  intervention across central Chile (26 monitored reservoirs spanning the 2010–present
  megadrought) and estimate its effect on drought propagation and water-dependent land use
  using a national matched design (entropy balancing within Köppen × aridity strata; 21 of 24
  treated basins retained, effective control sample $\approx 91$), doubly-robust matched ATT,
  forcing-conditioned difference-in-differences, and randomization inference. Across every
  operational pathway (meteorological-to-hydrological drought transmission, evapotranspiration
  buffering, and irrigated-area expansion), the treatment effect brackets zero once siting is
  matched out. A within-basin placebo comparing regulated downstream reaches against physically
  unregulated upstream reaches of the same dammed basins (15 of 21 basins) is the cleanest
  within-design falsification: the apparent
  national buffering signal (slope gap −0.18) is as strong upstream as downstream and
  collapses to $\approx −0.03$ within climate region (p_perm = 0.39), the signature of an
  aridity-gradient confound, not regulation. Refill efficiency is undiminished while the whole
  storage band drifts downward, a pattern consistent with declining water supply rather than a
  loss of storage or buffering capacity. Reservoirs in Chile thus appear to mark pre-existing,
  siting-determined vulnerability rather than make resilience; once siting is accounted for, the
  operational case for storage expansion as drought protection is not supported by these data.
keywords:

  - drought propagation
